title: Lab — Map One Week Against What You'd Delegate
description: Take a real or realistic week of your own coding work and sort it against this module's framework, with a stated reason for every call.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the pattern-density and verifiability framework to your own real work
Produce a one-page delegation map with a defensible reason for every task

contentSections.body: Priya's rate limiter and the discount-stacking rule are worked examples. Your own week of work is the real test of whether the framework holds up outside a lesson — because your actual tasks won't arrive pre-sorted into 'obviously good fit' and 'obviously bad fit' the way examples do.

contentSections.title: Your delegation map
contentSections.brief: Pick a real week of your coding work — the most recent one you can recall in enough detail, or if you're between projects, a realistic week built from tasks you actually do. List what you worked on, sort each task by fit using this module's framework, and write down your reason for every single call — including the ones that don't feel obvious.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-page delegation map: every task from the week, sorted into delegate / direct-with-review / do-yourself, with a one-line stated reason for each.

stages.title: Inventory the week
stages.instructions: List every discrete coding task from the week — aim for 12-20 items. Break big efforts into the actual decisions and translations inside them, the way this module broke Priya's six minutes into six separate things. 'Built the rate limiter' is one line; 'decided the key, wrote the loop, caught the wrong key, tested the boundary' is four, and the four are what you're actually sorting.
stages.checkpoint: You have a list of specific tasks, each one small enough to sort on its own — not a handful of project-sized entries.

stages.title: Sort by pattern density and verifiability
stages.instructions: For each task, ask the two questions from the module: is there a dense, well-worn pattern to draw from, and is the result checkable? Sort into delegate / direct-with-review / do-yourself, and write one line per task stating which of the two questions drove the call — or, for anything genuinely close, what made it close.
stages.checkpoint: Every task has a category and a stated reason that references pattern density, verifiability, or both — not a gut feeling with no basis given.

stages.title: Write the one-page map and self-check
stages.instructions: Compress the sorted list into a one-page map someone else on your team could read and understand your reasoning from, without you in the room to explain it. Then self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: It fits on one page, every task has a category and a reason, and a colleague reading it cold would understand why each call was made.

rubric.criterion: Tasks are specific, not project-sized
rubric.meets: Each item is a single decision or translation small enough to sort on its own — the way the module's worked examples broke a session into individual pieces.

rubric.criterion: Every call has a stated reason
rubric.meets: The reason references pattern density, verifiability, or both — not 'felt risky' or 'seemed fine' with nothing under it.

rubric.criterion: At least one call is genuinely close, and says so
rubric.meets: Real weeks have ambiguous tasks. If every single one lands cleanly in one category, the categories probably aren't being applied carefully.

rubric.criterion: The do-yourself category isn't empty
rubric.meets: If everything from a real week is delegate or direct-with-review, that's worth questioning rather than taking as a clean result.

rubric.criterion: It fits on one page
rubric.meets: A colleague could read the whole thing in two minutes and follow the reasoning without asking you to explain it.

contentSections.body: The framework is only useful once it survives contact with a real, messy week — including the tasks that don't sort cleanly.

title: Checkpoint — What Actually Changes
description: Ten questions from this module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

questions.prompt: In Priya's rate-limiter session, what moved to the AI tool?

options.label: The mechanical translation of an already-made decision into working code
Deciding what correct behavior looks like
Catching when the diff doesn't match the spec

questions.explanation: The typing moved. The decisions about correctness, and the noticing when a diff doesn't match them, stayed with Priya the whole time.

questions.prompt: Why did an AI tool rename unrelated variables in a file it was only asked to add a rate limiter to?

options.label: It decided the surrounding code needed tidying
It continued a statistically common pattern from PRs like this one — not a judgment call
A bug caused it to edit outside the requested scope

questions.explanation: There's no evaluation step where the tool forms an opinion about your file. Unscoped changes ride along because they're common in the training data, not because they were considered.

questions.prompt: An unscoped, ambiguous prompt gets filled with...

options.label: Whatever's most statistically common across general code, which may not match your codebase
A random choice between plausible options
Nothing — the tool leaves ambiguous parts for you to fill in

questions.explanation: Ambiguity isn't neutral. It resolves to the common default, which is why naming your specific convention changes the outcome rather than just being polite.

questions.prompt: What actually predicts whether a task is a good fit to delegate?

options.label: How difficult the task would be for an experienced human to write quickly
Pattern density and whether the result is checkable
Whether the task involves a well-known algorithm

questions.explanation: A hard-looking regex can be a great fit; a trivial-sounding, unwritten business rule can be a terrible one. Human difficulty doesn't track the actual predictor.

questions.prompt: Why was the discount-stacking rule a bad fit to delegate, even though it's a one-sentence rule?

options.label: It exists nowhere the tool could see it, so there was no pattern to complete correctly, only a plausible-sounding default
Discount logic is inherently too complex for AI tools
The tool should have asked a clarifying question first

questions.explanation: No amount of test coverage or careful phrasing recovers a constraint that was never supplied. The fix has to happen before generation, by putting the rule in the prompt.

questions.prompt: Two AI-generated functions do the same job. One has clean names and a confident docstring; the other doesn't. What can you conclude about which is more likely correct?

options.label: The documented one is more likely correct
Nothing — fluency and correctness are separate properties produced by the same process
The undocumented one is more likely correct, being less embellished

questions.explanation: A wrong implementation gets explained just as fluently as a right one. Trace an uncovered case by hand — the currency parser's negative-amount gap, for instance — rather than reading polish as evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement would hold up as a defensible account of having reviewed a change?

options.label: "I read through it and it looked fine"
"I traced the specific boundary case the spec depended on and confirmed the behavior"
"The AI wrote it and it's usually reliable"

questions.explanation: A defensible answer names what was specifically checked and what it confirmed. The other two describe an activity, or authorship, without saying what was actually established.

questions.prompt: A bug traced to AI-generated code ships after a developer's "quick read-through." Where does responsibility sit?

options.label: Shared between the developer and the tool vendor
With the developer who merged it — the same rule as when a human approves a colleague's PR
Nowhere in particular — an accepted cost of using AI tools

questions.explanation: Merging is the assertion, regardless of who typed the diff. This isn't a new rule for AI tools — it's the existing rule for anyone who approves a change.

questions.prompt: In the postmortem case study, what turned out to be the useful question, once the room stopped debating fault?

options.label: Whether AI-generated code should be banned from touching null handling
What the quick read-through actually checked, and what this specific change needed checked
Whether Dana should be removed from the review rotation

questions.explanation: The specific gap — no test exercised the broken null case — is what a useful postmortem finds. A blanket policy is either too broad to survive contact with real work or too narrow to have caught this bug.

questions.prompt: Marcus wrote the same rate limiter by hand, taking 35 minutes instead of Priya's 6. What does the module say about the difference between their outcomes?

options.label: Marcus's version is more trustworthy because he typed every character
Both shipped correct code — the decisions and the catching of errors were the same work either way, just with or without the typing
Priya's version is riskier because it was reviewed too quickly

questions.explanation: Both developers made the same decisions and would have had to catch the same kinds of errors. The difference is where the ninety seconds versus thirty-five minutes went, not the rigor behind the result.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Why "make it better" produces nothing you can check
description: A spec is only useful if some output could fail it. Vague requests don't just risk a bad result — they remove the ability to tell a good one from a bad one.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an unfalsifiable request produces output nobody can review against a standard
Rewrite a vague request as a falsifiable claim

contentSections.body: A tech lead prompts: "make the checkout flow better." The diff that comes back touches button styling, reorders two form steps, and rewrites three error messages. Nothing in it is obviously wrong. Nobody can say whether it succeeded, either — because "better" never named a state the code could fail to be in.

A specification is only doing work if some possible output would fail it. "Reduce checkout from 3 steps to 1 for a returning customer with saved payment info" can fail — a diff that leaves 3 steps in place fails it, visibly. "Make it better" can't fail, which means it also can't succeed in any way you could point at. Review against it collapses into a vibe check, and different reviewers looking at the same diff will disagree about whether it worked, because there was never anything specific to agree or disagree about.

contentSections.scenario: Six phrases a request for checkout improvements might contain.
contentSections.question: Select every phrase that names a state the resulting code could actually fail to be in.

items.label: "Reduce the flow from 3 steps to 1 for returning customers with saved payment info"
"Should feel smoother to use"
"A first-time customer completes checkout in under 3 minutes, measured from cart to confirmation"
"Uses modern UX patterns"
"Reduces the billing form from 9 fields to 5 by inferring city/state from zip code"
"Is more user-friendly overall"

explanation.one-step: Falsifiable. Count the steps in the resulting flow; the claim is true or false with no further judgment needed.
explanation.feel-smoother: Not falsifiable. 'Feel' names a subjective impression with no state in the code to check it against — two reviewers could look at the same result and disagree forever.
explanation.under-3s: Falsifiable. Time it. The claim names a measurement and a threshold.
explanation.modern-ux: Not falsifiable. 'Modern' has no fixed definition and changes meaning depending on who's asked — it names a vibe, not a state.
explanation.fewer-fields: Falsifiable. Count the fields; check whether city/state actually get inferred from the zip code, rather than just removed.
explanation.user-friendly: Not falsifiable, for the same reason as 'better' in the hook — it names an overall impression, not a checkable state.

contentSections.synthesis: The falsifiable ones all share a shape: a specific measurement or count, and a threshold or exact value. The unfalsifiable ones are impressions dressed as requirements — real feelings, sometimes even correct ones, but not something a diff can be checked against.

contentSections.body: A spec only does work if some output could fail it. 'Better,' 'clean,' and 'user-friendly' fail nothing, which means they can't confirm anything either.

The practical cost shows up as a review loop with no stopping condition. A reviewer sends back "still not quite right, try again" for the third time. The fourth attempt might genuinely be excellent — there's no way to know, because nothing was ever named that a fourth attempt could be checked against. The loop isn't evidence the tool is struggling. It's evidence nobody defined what winning looks like.

contentSections.scenario: Four rounds of "try again" on the same component, with no criteria ever stated. On round five, the output is functionally identical to round two, which was also rejected.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation?

options.label: The tool forgot what it generated in round two
There's no stable target being aimed at — each round is judged against whatever the reviewer feels in the moment, which can land differently on identical output
AI generation is inherently random, so identical-looking output is a coincidence with no cause

feedback.no-target: Right. Without a written target, 'right' is being reconstructed fresh each round from whatever the reviewer's mood or attention happens to produce that day — which can genuinely reject the same code twice for different unstated reasons.
feedback.tool-forgot: The tool has no memory obligation to enforce consistency with an unstated target across sessions, but that's not what's happening here — the target was never written down in the first place, so there's nothing to have forgotten.
feedback.random-noise: Generation does have some randomness, but 'functionally identical' output being rejected once and not needing to be rejected the other time isn't explained by that alone — it's explained by there being no fixed thing being checked against.

contentSections.concept: A review loop needs a target that exists independent of any single round, or it can reject good output and accept bad output based on nothing more durable than the reviewer's state that day. Writing three or four checkable criteria before the next round gives both the tool and the reviewer the same fixed thing to aim at and check against — which is usually what actually ends loops like this, not a better model.

contentSections.body: A review loop with no stated target can reject good work and approve bad work by accident. Name the target before round two, not after round four.

title: Inputs, outputs, and the cases at the edges
description: The three-part discipline that turns 'find the median' from a request with three silent design decisions into one with none.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which parts of a task description leave input, output, or edge-case behavior undecided
Write a complete inputs/outputs/edge-cases section for a function

contentSections.body: "Write a function that finds the median of a list of numbers." Reasonable-sounding, four seconds to write, and it leaves at least three decisions completely open: what happens on an empty list, what happens on an even-length list (average the two middle values, or return the lower one — both defensible, both different), and whether non-numeric entries raise or get silently skipped.

The discipline that closes all three at once has three parts, always in the same order: **inputs** (type, shape, and what's explicitly not valid), **outputs** (type, and precisely what it means), **edge cases at the boundaries** (empty, single-element, the smallest and largest 'normal' inputs, and anything that isn't obviously in-range). None of these are extra — they're the parts of the task description that were silently missing, not additions to it.

contentSections.intro: Fill in the median function's spec, one decision at a time.

options.label: A non-empty list of numbers; raise ValueError on an empty list
options.value: non-empty list of numbers; raise ValueError if empty

options.label: A list of numbers (unspecified about empty)

fields.correctValue: non-empty list of numbers; raise ValueError if empty

feedback.non-empty list of numbers; raise ValueEr: Right — this closes the empty-list ambiguity by naming both the constraint and what happens if it's violated, rather than leaving 'a list' to imply anything is acceptable.
feedback.a list of numbers: This is the version from the hook — it reads as a spec but leaves the empty-list decision exactly as open as the one-sentence request did.

fields.prompt: What does an even-length list return?

options.label: The average of the two middle values, after sorting
options.value: average of the two middle values after sorting

options.label: Unspecified — whichever the implementation finds natural

fields.correctValue: average of the two middle values after sorting

feedback.average of the two middle values after s: Right — this is the standard statistical definition, and stating it removes the second real design choice from the hook.
feedback.unspecified: This is exactly the gap that produces two different, both-plausible implementations depending on which convention the tool's training leaned toward that day.

fields.prompt: What's the output type and meaning?

options.label: A float — the middle value (odd length) or average of the two middle values (even length), after sorting
options.value: a float: middle value (odd) or average of two middle values (even), after sorting

options.label: "The median"

fields.correctValue: a float: middle value (odd) or average of two middle values (even), after sorting

feedback.a float: middle value (odd) or average o: Right — this pins the type (a float, even for a list of ints, since averaging two middle values can produce a fraction) and restates the meaning precisely enough to implement from.
feedback.the median: This just repeats the function's name back as its own definition — it doesn't say what type comes out or how it's computed, which is the whole point of an output contract.

contentSections.synthesis: Three fields, three decisions that the original one-sentence request left to chance. Nothing here is more code than the request implied — it's the same function, with the parts that were silently undecided now written down.

contentSections.body: Inputs, outputs, edge cases — in that order, every time. Each one closes a decision the bare task description left open.

contentSections.problem: Write the inputs/outputs/edge-cases section for a function that parses one row of a CSV file (a string) into a list of string fields, handling quoted fields that may contain commas.

steps.label: Input
steps.work: A single string representing one CSV row, no trailing newline. Fields may be quoted with double quotes; a quoted field may contain commas and escaped double quotes (`""`). Not valid: a string with an unterminated quote.
steps.why: Naming exactly what 'quoted' allows (commas, escaped quotes) is what stops a naive implementation that only splits on unquoted commas and breaks on the first quoted comma it sees.

steps.label: Output
steps.work: A list of strings, one per field, in order, with surrounding quotes stripped and escaped quotes (`""`) unescaped to a single `"`.
steps.why: Stating that quotes are stripped and escapes are resolved — not just 'the fields' — is what prevents an implementation that returns fields still wrapped in their original quote characters.

steps.label: Edge case: empty row
steps.work: An empty string input returns a list with one empty string, `['']` — matching how a single trailing comma-free empty line is typically read, not an empty list.
steps.why: This is genuinely ambiguous without a stated convention — `[]` and `['']` are both defensible, and callers will write different code depending on which one they get.

steps.label: Edge case: unterminated quote
steps.work: Raise a `ValueError` naming the row content, rather than returning a partial or best-effort result.
steps.why: Silently returning something plausible for malformed input is worse than failing loudly, because a caller can't distinguish 'parsed correctly' from 'parsed something.'

faded.problem: Now the earlier module's dedupe function: remove duplicate strings from a list, case-sensitively, keeping the first occurrence's position and casing. Fill in the spec.

blanks.prompt: Input type and constraint (a few words)?
accept: a list of strings, any length
blanks.why: Naming the element type rules out ambiguity about whether non-string entries are allowed.

blanks.prompt: What determines whether two entries are duplicates? (a few words)
blanks.why: Without this line, 'duplicate' could silently mean case-insensitive equality instead, changing which entries get removed.
This is the exact requirement a naive `set()`-based implementation drops silently, as covered in the earlier module.

blanks.prompt: Edge case: empty list input — what's returned?
blanks.why: Stating the empty case explicitly, even when the 'obvious' answer is the one everyone would guess, is what makes the spec complete rather than merely likely-correct.

contentSections.procedure: Input contract, output contract and meaning, then every edge case named with its specific behavior — never 'handled correctly,' always the actual value or the actual exception. A spec section is done when someone who has never seen the task could implement it and get exactly your function, not a plausible cousin of it.

contentSections.body: A spec is done when a stranger could implement your exact function from it, not a plausible cousin of it.

title: Stating the constraints a tool cannot infer
description: Dependencies, security assumptions, performance bounds, and house style all live outside the task description — and outside the tool's reach unless you put them in.

learningObjectives.text: Categorize constraints that a bare task description cannot supply
Diagnose a generated change that violated a constraint nobody stated

contentSections.body: "Write a function that fetches a URL and caches the result." What comes back: `node-fetch`, which isn't in `package.json`, and an in-memory `Map` with no expiry, while every other cache in the codebase is Redis with a TTL. Nothing about the request was wrong. Nothing about the answer was unreasonable in general. It just didn't match this specific repo, because nothing that would have told it so was ever supplied.

Four categories of constraint live entirely outside a bare task description: **dependency and library limits** (what's actually installed, what's actually allowed), **security assumptions** (is this input trusted or does it cross a trust boundary), **performance bounds** (what throughput or memory ceiling this actually needs to meet), and **house style** (the codebase's own conventions for errors, exports, naming). None of these are inferable from 'fetch a URL and cache it' — they live in `package.json`, in the deployment topology, in a style guide, or in a pattern the tool would only see if you showed it.
Dependencies, security, performance, style — none of them are visible from a bare request. Naming them is the spec's job, not the tool's guess.

contentSections.scenario: A function was originally written to parse configuration files bundled at build time — trusted, internal input. It skips validating field lengths and doesn't escape anything, because nothing malicious could reach it. Six months later, the same function is reused, unchanged, to parse a user-uploaded config file on a public endpoint.
contentSections.question: What's the actual failure here, in terms of what a spec would have needed to state?

options.label: The trust boundary moved when the function got reused, and nothing forced anyone to re-specify or re-check the security assumption that no longer held
The original code should have had more unit tests
The developer who reused it should have just known it was unsafe, from experience

feedback.trust-boundary-moved: Right. The function's original spec (implicit, in this case, and never written down) assumed trusted input. Nothing about reusing the function forced a re-check of that assumption against its new context, because the assumption was never stated anywhere for anyone to notice had stopped holding.
feedback.should-have-tested: More tests against the original trusted-input assumption wouldn't have caught this — the function worked exactly as designed for its original context. The gap is a missing constraint, not a missing test.
feedback.user-should-know: Relying on someone 'just knowing' an unstated assumption six months and a different context later is exactly the failure mode a written constraint exists to prevent. It's not a character flaw to have missed it; it's a spec that never named the thing that mattered.

contentSections.mechanism: A security assumption that's never written down travels with the code as an invisible property, and invisible properties don't survive being moved into a new context. The fix isn't better memory — it's stating the trust boundary explicitly wherever the function is specified: 'assumes input has already been validated by the upstream caller' or 'must independently validate — input may be untrusted.' Either one, written down, is something the next reuse can be checked against instead of silently inherited.

contentSections.body: An unstated security assumption travels invisibly with reused code. State the trust boundary explicitly, or it silently stops holding the moment the context changes.

title: Acceptance criteria as the first thing you write
description: Criteria written before the prompt keep review honest. Criteria written after looking at the code tend to bend toward whatever the code already does.

learningObjectives.text: Sequence a spec-first workflow that keeps acceptance criteria independent of the generated output
Write given/when/then acceptance criteria for a stated behavior

contentSections.body: A team that writes given/when/then acceptance criteria before ever opening the AI tool gets first-draft-correct output far more often than a team that prompts first and judges afterward. Not because the criteria make the prompt more persuasive — because they make the review honest. Criteria written against code you're already looking at have a way of quietly becoming a description of what the code does, rather than a check on it.

Given/when/then names three things: a starting state (**given**), an action (**when**), and an observable result (**then**) — observable meaning something a caller or a test could actually see, not an internal implementation detail. "Given a file of exactly 10,485,761 bytes, when uploaded, then the server responds 413 with a JSON body naming the limit" is checkable by anyone, without needing to read the implementation. Writing these before prompting does two things at once: it sharpens the prompt itself (the criteria *are* the constraints), and it gives review something to check off, one line at a time, instead of a general impression to form.

contentSections.question: Put the spec-first workflow in the order that keeps the criteria honest.
steps: Write acceptance criteria in given/when/then form, before touching the AI tool
Write the prompt, including the criteria as explicit constraints
Generate the code
Check the output against each criterion individually
For anything that fails, revise with that specific gap named, not a general 'try again'
contentSections.explanation: The criteria have to exist before the prompt, or they risk being reverse-engineered from whatever the tool happens to produce — which defeats the entire point of having an independent check. Checking each criterion individually rather than reading the whole diff for a general impression is what turns a vague 'looks right' into a list someone else could audit without re-deriving your judgment from scratch. And when something fails, naming the specific gap — not 'still not quite right' — is what keeps the next round from becoming the same unanchored loop from the module's first lesson.

contentSections.body: Criteria written before the prompt exist independent of the output. Criteria written after tend to describe whatever the code already does.

The habit that makes given/when/then actually useful, rather than just formal-sounding: name the exact boundary, both sides of it, and what the caller actually observes — a status code, a returned value, a raised exception — not an internal implementation detail nobody outside the function could check.

contentSections.intro: Build one acceptance criterion for 'reject file uploads over 10MB,' field by field.

options.label: A file of exactly 10,485,761 bytes (one byte over the 10MB limit)
A large file

feedback.a file of exactly 10,485,761 bytes: Right — naming the exact byte count one past the limit is what tests the boundary itself, which is exactly where an off-by-one hides.
feedback.a large file: 'Large' doesn't specify whether it's testing the boundary or just 'obviously huge,' and an implementation could pass this criterion while getting the exact boundary wrong.

options.label: The server responds 413 with a JSON body naming the size limit
options.value: responds 413 with a JSON body naming the size limit

options.label: The upload is rejected

fields.correctValue: responds 413 with a JSON body naming the size limit

feedback.responds 413 with a JSON body naming the: Right — a specific status code and response shape is something a caller, or an automated test, can check without reading the server's internals.
feedback.the upload is rejected: 'Rejected' could mean a 413, a 400, a silent connection drop, or a 500 — all technically 'not accepted,' and all producing very different experiences for whoever's calling this endpoint.

fields.prompt: What's the matching criterion for the other side of the boundary?

options.label: Given a file of exactly 10,485,760 bytes (the limit itself), when uploaded, then it's accepted
No matching criterion needed — one side is enough

feedback.given exactly 10,485,760 bytes, then acc: Right — testing only the rejected side leaves open whether the limit is actually 10MB or the implementation is off by one in the other direction, silently rejecting files that should be accepted.
feedback.none needed: A boundary only means something when both sides of it are checked — otherwise 'over 10MB is rejected' could be satisfied by an implementation that also rejects files at 9MB, and nothing here would catch it.

contentSections.synthesis: Exact boundary value, an observable result, and the matching criterion on the other side. Three small decisions, and together they close off the two ways an upload-size check most commonly ships wrong.

contentSections.body: Test both sides of every boundary, and state what the caller actually observes — not just 'it works,' but the exact status code or return value that would prove it.

title: Specs that survive being handed to someone else
description: A spec that works because you're filling its gaps from memory isn't done — it's a spec plus your head, and only one of those travels.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a spec is portable to someone with no memory of the original context
Revise a spec that passed for its author but failed for a teammate

contentSections.body: Your spec for the median function said the edge-case section "handles the empty list case." It worked fine for you — you remembered, from the conversation where you wrote it, that empty should return `None`. A teammate reuses the same written spec a month later, in a fresh AI session with no memory of that conversation, and gets a function that raises `ValueError` instead. Nothing in the spec was technically false. It just wasn't actually written down.

The real test for a spec being done isn't whether it produces correct code for you. It's portability: would a stranger — or you, in six months, with zero memory of writing it — get the same result from the words on the page alone? "Handles the empty list case" names that a decision exists without recording what it was, which passes a casual glance while deferring the entire content of the spec to whoever's memory happens to be in the room that day.

contentSections.scenario: Six lines that might appear in a written spec's edge-case section.
contentSections.question: Select every line that would survive being handed to a teammate with no memory of the original conversation.

items.label: "Empty list: return None (not an exception)"
"Empty list: handled appropriately"
"Assumes input has already been validated by the calling service"
"Be careful with untrusted input"
"Cache entries expire after 300 seconds"
"Cache for a reasonable amount of time"

explanation.empty-none: Survives. States the exact return value — nothing left for a fresh reader to reconstruct from memory.
explanation.empty-handled: Doesn't survive. Names that a decision was made without recording it, which is functionally identical to not having a spec for this case at all.
explanation.auth-trusted: Survives. States the actual trust boundary, which is exactly the information a reuse six months later would need to catch the failure from an earlier lesson in this module.
explanation.auth-careful: Doesn't survive. 'Be careful' isn't an instruction a fresh reader — or a tool — can act on; it names a feeling, not a validation rule.
explanation.cache-ttl: Survives. A specific number a fresh implementation can match exactly.
explanation.cache-reasonable: Doesn't survive. 'Reasonable' was never a duration — every reader fills it in differently, which is exactly the caching bug from an earlier exercise in this module.

contentSections.synthesis: Every line that survives states an exact value, an exact boundary, or an exact assumption. Every line that doesn't survive gestures at the fact that a decision exists, without recording what the decision actually was — and a spec's whole job is recording decisions, not flagging that some were made.

contentSections.body: Portable means: a fresh reader with none of your memory gets the same result. 'Handled appropriately' fails that test regardless of how confident it sounds.

contentSections.title: Fixing a spec that failed a teammate

contentSections.body: When a spec fails this way, the fix is never to make it longer — it's to make the specific gap concrete. "Handles the empty list case" and "empty list: return None (not an exception)" are nearly the same length. Only one of them can be implemented two different, incompatible ways by two competent people reading the same words.

contentSections.question: Quick check: would a line reading "validates the input thoroughly" pass the portability test — could a stranger implement identically from it?
contentSections.hint: What would two different, both-competent readers each build from that sentence?
contentSections.answer: No. 'Thoroughly' names no specific rule — one reader might check for type only, another might add length limits, format checks, and sanitization. Two competent implementations from the same sentence could differ enormously, which is the definition of a spec line that hasn't actually specified anything. The fix is the same as every other example in this lesson: replace the adverb with the actual rule — 'rejects any string over 255 characters, or containing a null byte, with a ValidationError.'

contentSections.body: If two competent readers could implement your spec two incompatible ways, it hasn't specified anything yet — no matter how thorough it sounds.

title: Practice — Rewrite Eight Vague Requests as Executable Specs
description: Eight drills across the module's skills: spotting what's unfalsifiable, naming edge cases, sorting hidden constraints, and writing criteria that bind.

learningObjectives.text: Rewrite vague requests as falsifiable, complete specs at speed
Distinguish a spec that would survive a handoff from one that wouldn't

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing expires.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Spec a Feature, Then Have It Built From the Spec Alone
description: Write acceptance criteria and a complete spec for a small real feature, run it through an AI tool exactly once, and check every criterion against what came back.

learningObjectives.text: Write acceptance criteria before prompting, and a complete inputs/outputs/edge-cases/constraints spec
Check generated output against every stated criterion individually

contentSections.body: This is the module's whole argument, run for real: write the spec before you look at any code, generate exactly once, and see how many of your own criteria the first draft actually meets. The gap between what you get and what you specified is the most honest feedback you'll get on how complete your spec really was.

contentSections.title: Spec first, build once
contentSections.brief: Pick a small, real feature or function you actually need — from a personal project, a work backlog, or something you've been meaning to write. Write its acceptance criteria and full spec before opening an AI tool. Then generate it once, with no follow-up clarification round, and check the result against every criterion.
contentSections.deliverable: The written spec (acceptance criteria plus inputs/outputs/edge cases/constraints), the generated code, and a checklist showing each acceptance criterion marked met, not met, or explained.

stages.title: Write acceptance criteria first
stages.instructions: Before writing anything else, write 3-5 acceptance criteria in given/when/then form for your chosen feature. Include at least one boundary case with both sides tested, the way the module's upload-size example did.
stages.checkpoint: You have 3-5 given/when/then criteria, written before any spec detail or any prompt, with at least one boundary tested on both sides.

stages.title: Write the full spec
stages.instructions: Write the inputs/outputs/edge-cases section, then name any constraints an AI tool couldn't infer — dependencies, security assumptions, performance bounds, house style — that actually apply to your feature. Skip any category that genuinely doesn't apply, but say so rather than leaving it silently absent.
stages.checkpoint: Every input, output, and edge case has a stated value or behavior — nothing says 'handled appropriately.' Every applicable constraint category is addressed or explicitly marked not applicable.

stages.title: Generate once, no follow-up
stages.instructions: Turn the spec into a prompt and generate the code in a single round — no back-and-forth clarification, no second attempt yet. This is the part of the lab that tests the spec, not your ability to iterate your way to a good result.
stages.checkpoint: You have one generated diff, produced from a single prompt built directly from your written spec.

stages.title: Check every criterion, and self-check the spec itself
stages.instructions: Go through each acceptance criterion individually and mark it met, not met, or explain why it's ambiguous. For anything not met or ambiguous, note whether the failure traces back to a gap in the spec (something you didn't specify) or a genuine miss by the tool (something you did specify, correctly, that the output still got wrong) — these call for different fixes. Then self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: Every criterion has a verdict and, where it wasn't cleanly met, a stated cause — spec gap or tool miss.

rubric.criterion: Acceptance criteria exist before any code was generated
rubric.meets: Written and dated before the first prompt, not reconstructed afterward from the diff.

rubric.criterion: Every stated value is exact, not a placeholder
rubric.meets: No 'handled appropriately,' 'reasonable,' or 'as needed' anywhere in the spec — real values, real thresholds, real exceptions.

rubric.criterion: At least one boundary is tested on both sides
rubric.meets: A criterion exists for both just-inside and just-outside the same limit.

rubric.criterion: Applicable hidden-constraint categories are addressed
rubric.meets: Dependencies, security, performance, and style are each either specified or explicitly marked not applicable — none silently skipped.

rubric.criterion: Every criterion has a clear verdict
rubric.meets: Met, not met, or ambiguous — with a one-line reason, for all of them, not just the ones that failed.

rubric.criterion: Failures are traced to a cause
rubric.meets: Each unmet criterion says whether the spec had a gap or the tool missed something the spec correctly stated.

contentSections.body: The gap between your spec and the first draft is the most honest measurement of how complete the spec actually was — more honest than a second round would have been.

title: Checkpoint — The Executable Spec
description: Ten questions: five from this module, five from What Actually Changes. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions and the previous module's, without looking them up

questions.prompt: Why does "make it better" fail as a spec?

options.label: It names no state the code could fail to be in, so nothing could be checked against it
It's too short to give the tool enough to work with
It should have included a code example

questions.explanation: A spec only does work if some output could fail it. 'Better' can't fail, so it also can't be confirmed — review collapses into opinion.

questions.prompt: The median function example left three decisions open. Which of these was one of them?

options.label: Whether an even-length list averages the two middle values or returns the lower one
What programming language to use
Whether the function should have a docstring

questions.explanation: Even-length behavior, empty-list behavior, and non-numeric input were the three genuine, both-plausible ambiguities the bare request left open.

questions.prompt: Which category of constraint explains why a generated caching function used node-fetch and an unbounded Map instead of the project's existing Redis client?

options.label: A dependency and house-style constraint that was never supplied in the prompt or context
A bug in the tool that ignores existing code
node-fetch and unbounded caching are simply always the correct default

questions.prompt: Why write acceptance criteria before prompting rather than after seeing the generated code?

options.label: Criteria written against code already in front of you tend to bend toward describing what that code does
It's required by most AI tools' input format
It makes the prompt shorter

questions.explanation: Writing criteria first keeps them independent of any particular output, which is what lets them actually catch a gap instead of rationalizing one away.

questions.prompt: A spec says "handles the empty list case." What's wrong with this line?

options.label: It names that a decision exists without recording what the decision actually was, so it won't survive being handed to someone else
It's too specific for a high-level spec
Nothing — it clearly covers the empty-list case

questions.explanation: A teammate with no memory of the original conversation could implement this two incompatible ways. The fix is naming the exact return value, not writing more words around the gap.

questions.prompt: In Priya's rate-limiter session, what stayed with her rather than moving to the tool?

options.label: Deciding the counter should key on user id, and catching that the diff didn't
Typing the counter increment logic
Wiring the middleware into the route

questions.explanation: The decisions about correctness, and noticing when the output doesn't match them, are exactly what didn't move to the tool.

questions.prompt: Why did a coding tool rename unrelated variables in a file it was only asked to add a rate limiter to?

options.label: It continued a statistically common pattern from similar PRs, not a considered judgment
It decided the surrounding code needed cleanup
A bug caused it to edit outside scope

questions.explanation: There's no evaluation step where the tool forms an opinion about your file — unscoped changes ride along because they're common in training data.

questions.prompt: What actually predicts whether a task is a good fit to delegate to an AI tool?

options.label: Pattern density and whether the result is checkable
How difficult the task looks to an experienced human
Whether the task involves a well-known algorithm

questions.explanation: A hard-looking regex can be a great fit; a trivial-sounding unwritten business rule can be a terrible one.

questions.prompt: Two AI-generated functions do the same job; one has clean names and confident documentation, the other doesn't. What can you conclude about which is more likely correct?

options.label: Nothing — fluency and correctness are separate properties produced by the same process
The documented one is more likely correct
The undocumented one is more likely correct

questions.explanation: A wrong implementation gets explained just as fluently as a right one — polish is not independent evidence of correctness.

questions.prompt: A bug traced to AI-generated code ships after a developer's "quick read-through." Where does responsibility sit?

options.label: With the developer who merged it, the same as when a human approves a colleague's PR
Shared between the developer and the tool vendor
Nowhere in particular

questions.explanation: Merging is the assertion, regardless of who typed the diff.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The tool knows nothing about your codebase unless you show it
description: A fresh session has no standing access to your repo, your history, or last week's conversation — only what's actually placed in front of it, this time.

learningObjectives.text: Explain that a coding tool's context is limited to what's explicitly supplied in a given session
Distinguish what actually carries into a new session from what a developer might assume carries over

contentSections.title: A stranger who's never seen your repo

contentSections.body: A developer opens a fresh AI coding session and prompts: "add a new field to the User model, following our patterns." No file attached, nothing pasted. What comes back is a plausible-looking field addition — camelCase, a generic validator, a docstring — that matches none of this repo's actual conventions, because nothing about this repo's actual conventions was ever placed in front of the tool.

A coding session's context is, literally, everything the tool has to work with for that conversation — and by default that's exactly what was typed or attached, nothing more. It has no standing access to your filesystem, your git history, your Slack, or a conversation from yesterday, unless something specific grants and points it at exactly that. Treating a new session like a colleague who's worked in this codebase for years is the single most common way a spec-first workflow still produces output that ignores conventions the developer assumed were 'obviously' known.

contentSections.scenario: Two developers ask an AI tool the identical prompt: "add a `deactivatedAt` field to the User model." One pastes the existing User model file first. The other doesn't. The first gets a field matching the file's exact naming and null-handling convention. The second gets a plausible-looking field that uses a different naming style and a different null convention.
contentSections.question: Why did identical prompts produce different results?

options.label: The only actual difference between the two sessions was what was placed in the context — the prompt text alone was never going to carry the repo's specific conventions
Generation is inherently random, so this is just noise
The second developer must have been using a less capable model

feedback.context-difference: Right. The prompts were identical; the contexts weren't. The file that was pasted is the only variable that actually changed between the two sessions, and it's exactly the thing that determined whether the output matched this specific repo.
feedback.randomness: There's some variation between runs of any prompt, but this isn't that — the two outputs differ in exactly the dimension the pasted file would have constrained (naming, null-handling), which is a systematic effect, not noise.
feedback.second-session-worse-model: Nothing about the model changed between the two sessions. The variable that changed is the one this lesson is about: what was actually shown.

contentSections.mechanism: There's no implicit channel by which a coding tool learns your repo's conventions — it isn't inferred from the prompt's wording, and it isn't inherited from 'being a coding tool.' The only things a given session has to work with are what's explicitly in its context: pasted text, attached files, and — as later lessons in this module cover — a project instruction file specifically built to be auto-loaded. Everything else, no matter how well-known it is to you, is invisible.

contentSections.body: Nothing about your repo is visible to a session unless it's explicitly placed there. 'Our patterns' means nothing to a tool that's never seen a single file from this repo.

The practical habit: treat every new session as a stranger, even if it's technically 'the same tool' you talked to an hour ago. A handful of things genuinely do carry forward automatically — most importantly, a project instruction file the tool is specifically built to read at the start of a session, which the rest of this module builds toward. Everything else — a convention explained out loud last week, a Slack thread, yesterday's separate conversation — has to be re-supplied, every time, or assumed absent.

contentSections.scenario: Six things that might or might not be visible to a fresh AI coding session working in a project directory.
contentSections.question: Select every one of these the tool would actually have access to, with nothing extra done by the developer.

items.label: A CLAUDE.md or equivalent project instruction file in the project root
The fact that the convention was explained to a coworker out loud last week
A file explicitly pasted or attached into this conversation
The Slack thread where the convention was originally agreed
A file sitting in the same directory that was never shown or pointed at
The conversation history from a completely separate, earlier session

explanation.instruction-file: Visible. This is the one genuine exception to 'nothing carries over automatically' — a project instruction file is specifically built to be auto-loaded, which is exactly why later lessons in this module treat it as worth investing in.
explanation.coworker-explain: Invisible. Spoken context has no path into a coding session at all, no matter how recently or clearly it was communicated.
explanation.pasted-file: Visible. Whatever's actually placed in the conversation is what the tool has to work with — this is the direct, manual version of giving it context.
explanation.slack-thread: Invisible. Same as the coworker conversation — a real discussion that settled something real, with zero automatic path into this session.
explanation.sibling-file: Invisible. Proximity in the filesystem isn't the same as being shown — a file the tool hasn't been pointed at might as well not exist for this conversation.
explanation.earlier-session: Invisible by default. A separate session doesn't automatically carry forward, which is the exact assumption that produced the field-naming mismatch in the diagnose-mechanism exercise.

contentSections.synthesis: One item on the list is visible automatically, and it's the one built specifically to be. Everything else needs to be manually placed in front of the tool, every session, or it's exactly as absent as if it had never existed.

contentSections.body: Treat every new session as a stranger who's never seen your repo — because, except for an auto-loaded instruction file, that's exactly what it is.

title: Choosing what to include: the files that actually constrain the answer
description: More context isn't automatically better context — the useful bundle is small and specific: the closest example, the type it must satisfy, the test it has to pass.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which files actually constrain a given change request
Assemble a minimal, targeted context bundle for an unfamiliar codebase

contentSections.title: Buried in the file that should have helped

contentSections.body: A developer, wanting to be thorough, pastes the entire 2,000-line `routes.ts` file plus three unrelated files into a prompt for a new `DELETE /orders/:id` endpoint. The output ignores the one existing DELETE endpoint's error-handling pattern — which was right there, on line 1,400 of the file that was pasted specifically to be safe.

The relevant pattern being present in the context isn't the same as it being prominent. A single relevant example surrounded by 1,999 lines of everything else, plus three more unrelated files, carries no particular weight over anything else in the bundle — the model has no way to know which part of a large dump actually matters unless the bundle itself signals it by being small and specific. The habit that actually works: include the closest existing analog, the type or interface the new code must satisfy, and — if tests matter — the test file for that analog. Leave out everything that doesn't directly constrain this specific change.

contentSections.intro: Choose the context bundle for adding `DELETE /orders/:id` to an Express API that already has DELETE endpoints for two other resources.

fields.prompt: What's the single most important file to include?

options.label: The existing DELETE endpoint for a similar resource (e.g. DELETE /products/:id)
The full routes.ts file with all 40 endpoints

feedback.the existing analogous DELETE endpoint: Right — the single closest existing example is the highest-value thing in the bundle, because it demonstrates the actual pattern rather than making the tool search for it inside a much larger file.
feedback.the full routes file: This is the routes.ts mistake from the hook — the relevant pattern is in there, but so is everything else, and nothing marks it as the important part.

fields.prompt: What else genuinely constrains the answer?

options.label: The Order type/interface the endpoint has to work with
The full type definitions for every resource in the app

feedback.the Order type definition: Right — this is the second file that actually constrains the shape of the code, without pulling in types the endpoint will never touch.
feedback.all type definitions: Everything not related to Order dilutes the bundle the same way the unrelated files did in the hook, for no benefit — the new endpoint doesn't need to know the shape of every other resource in the app.

fields.prompt: What belongs in the 'leave out' pile?

options.label: The three unrelated files pasted 'to be safe'
Nothing — more is always safer

feedback.the three unrelated files: Right — none of them constrain this specific endpoint, and including them is exactly what diluted the one relevant pattern in the hook's actual failure.
feedback.nothing, include everything: This is the instinct that produced the bug in the hook. 'More is safer' assumes context is free; it isn't — it's the difference between a signal standing out and a signal getting lost.

contentSections.synthesis: Two files, chosen because they specifically constrain this change, beat five files chosen because they might be relevant. The bundle that worked is smaller than the one that failed, not bigger.

contentSections.body: A relevant file buried in a large, mostly-irrelevant dump carries no special weight. The useful bundle is small and specifically targeted, not maximal.

In practice, the short list is almost always the same three kinds of file: the closest structural analog (something that already does what you're asking for, on a different resource or in a different place), the contract the new code has to satisfy (a type, an interface, a schema), and — when correctness matters — the test for the analog, as a pattern for the new test. Naming this list explicitly, before pasting anything, is what keeps a developer from defaulting to 'paste everything that might be related.'

contentSections.question: Quick check: for a change to an existing function's internal logic (no new type, no new endpoint), would the closest-analog file and the contract-file categories collapse into the same file?
contentSections.hint: If you're only changing what's inside one function, what else is there left to constrain besides the function's own current version?
contentSections.answer: Often yes — for an internal-logic-only change, the function's own current file frequently serves as both the analog (what it does now) and the contract (what it must keep satisfying, like its existing type signature and callers). The three-category list is a checklist to run through, not a rule that three separate files must always appear; sometimes one file answers more than one question, and forcing in extra files just to fill categories reintroduces the dilution problem from the module's opening example.

contentSections.body: The short list is almost always: the closest analog, the contract it must satisfy, and the test pattern to follow. Everything else is a judgment call about whether it actually constrains this change.

title: Conventions, house style, and the cost of not stating them
description: A shown example demonstrates a convention at every point in its own logic. A prose description can be true and still leave a specific case unstated.

learningObjectives.text: Compare the reliability of a shown example against a prose description for communicating a convention
Diagnose why a prose-described convention was only partially followed

contentSections.body: A codebase validates everything with a `Result<T, ValidationError>`, never by throwing. The prompt says, in prose: "follow our validation convention — we use Result types, not exceptions." The generated function returns a Result for every check except the very first one, which throws on the first invalid field. The instruction wasn't wrong. It just didn't happen to say what should happen at that specific point.

A prose description of a convention can be entirely true and still leave a case unstated — 'we use Result types' says nothing about the very first check in a function, because sentences don't automatically cover every point in a control flow the way an actual working example does. A shown file doesn't carry this specific risk: it either demonstrates the pattern at a given point or it doesn't, with no true-but-silent gap for a case to fall through. This doesn't make prose useless — it's often faster to write, and fine for conventions with no edge to hide in — but for anything with a real control-flow shape, a real example is the more reliable choice.

contentSections.scenario: The Result-type example above, with the prose instruction present and mostly followed, except for the first check in the function.
contentSections.question: Why did a true instruction still produce an incomplete result?

options.label: Sentences don't automatically cover every point in a function's control flow the way a full worked example does — the instruction was true and simply silent about this specific case
The tool ignored the instruction for the first check specifically
This shows prose instructions are useless and should never be used for conventions

feedback.prose-gap: Right. The bulk of the function does follow the instruction, which rules out it being ignored. What's missing is coverage of one specific case the sentence never happened to address — the exact shape of risk a prose description carries that a full example doesn't.
feedback.tool-ignored: If the instruction were being ignored, none of the function would follow it. Most of it does, which points at an incomplete instruction rather than a disregarded one.
feedback.prose-never-works: Too strong — prose works fine for conventions with no real edge to miss. The lesson is narrower: for anything with a control-flow shape (what happens first, what happens on failure), a shown example is more reliable, not that prose is worthless everywhere.

contentSections.mechanism: A description is a summary, and summaries are compressed by nature — they capture the general shape of a rule and, unless the author is unusually careful, quietly omit specific cases the author didn't think to mention. A working example has no such compression: every line either does or doesn't follow the pattern, at every point, because it's real code that actually ran. Reaching for a real file instead of another sentence is most valuable exactly where prose is most likely to have a silent gap — anywhere the convention depends on order, sequencing, or what happens first.

contentSections.body: A true description can still be incomplete about a case it never mentioned. A shown example can't be incomplete in quite the same way — it either demonstrates the behavior or it doesn't, everywhere in its own logic.

Neither is strictly better in every case. A one-line, no-edge-case rule — "use single quotes, not double" — is genuinely fine as prose; there's no control flow for a gap to hide in. The judgment call is proportional to how much sequencing or conditional behavior the convention actually has: the more shape a rule has, the more a real example earns its place over another paragraph of description.

contentSections.question: Quick check: does "use single quotes, not double" have the same risk of a silent gap as the Result-type convention did?
contentSections.hint: Does this rule depend on order, sequencing, or what happens first — the kind of shape that gave the Result-type description its blind spot?
contentSections.answer: No — this rule has no control-flow shape for a gap to hide in. It applies uniformly everywhere quotes appear, with no case like 'the first check' that a sentence could silently omit. That's exactly why it's fine as prose, and exactly why it's a different category from a convention like Result-type error handling, which depends on sequencing a sentence can describe truthfully while still leaving one point unaddressed.

contentSections.body: Simple, edge-free rules are fine as prose. Anything with real shape — order, conditionals, what happens first — is safer shown than described.

title: Project instruction files and what belongs in one
description: A good instruction file names commands, conventions, and prohibitions specific enough to check against. A bad one is a page of encouragement that constrains nothing.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish instruction-file content that constrains generated output from content that doesn't
Write a project instruction file section covering commands, conventions, and prohibitions

contentSections.body: One project's instruction file: forty lines opening with "we value clean, maintainable, well-tested code" and closing with "always write code you'd be proud of." Another project's: the exact test command, a named file demonstrating the error-handling convention, and one line flagging that the payments directory needs a second reviewer. The second one is a third the length and does actual work every time a session starts.

An instruction file is, in effect, a spec for the whole repo — and it fails or succeeds by the same test as any other spec from earlier in this module: does each line name something checkable? "Clean, maintainable code" can't fail, so it constrains nothing, the same as "make it better" constrained nothing three lessons ago. What belongs: the actual test and build commands, pointers to real files demonstrating real conventions (not prose re-descriptions of them), dependency and security defaults, and explicit prohibitions on sensitive areas. What doesn't: aspirational values statements, a re-hash of the README's project history, or anything a developer wouldn't actually check the output against.

contentSections.question: Quick check: would "always write code you'd be proud of" survive being rewritten as a falsifiable claim, the way earlier lessons rewrote vague specs?
contentSections.hint: Could two different, both-reasonable diffs be compared against this line and get different verdicts, with no further judgment call needed?
contentSections.answer: No — there's no version of this sentence that becomes checkable no matter how it's rephrased, because it names a feeling about the code rather than any property of it. Compare to 'never add a new dependency without asking first': that one can be checked directly against a diff. 'Proud of' can only ever be re-judged by feel, which is the same failure as 'make it better' wearing a different sentence.

contentSections.body: An instruction file is a spec for the whole repo. Every line has to name something checkable, or it's decoration that costs context budget for nothing.

A working instruction file typically covers four things, in roughly this order: the commands that actually run (test, build, lint — the exact invocation, not "run the tests"), the conventions that matter most for this repo (pointing at real files, per the previous lesson, rather than re-describing them), the constraints from three lessons ago — dependencies, security defaults, performance bounds, house style — that apply broadly rather than to one function, and explicit prohibitions: what the tool should flag instead of silently doing, and what areas need a human before anything ships.

contentSections.question: You're writing an instruction file from scratch for a repo you're joining. Put these steps in the order that produces the most useful file, not the longest one.
steps: Find the actual commands (test, build, lint) from the repo's own scripts or CI config, not from memory or assumption
Identify the one or two conventions most likely to get violated by someone unfamiliar with the repo, and point at real files demonstrating each
Name any repo-wide constraints — allowed dependencies, security defaults, performance bounds — that apply across most of the codebase
Name any areas that need a human before anything ships, and what the tool should do instead of shipping it silently
Cut anything that doesn't change what gets generated or reviewed
contentSections.explanation: Commands come first because they're the most mechanically checkable and the easiest to get exactly right from the repo's own config, rather than guessed. Conventions come next, prioritized by likelihood of violation rather than completeness — a file that tries to document every convention in the repo becomes exactly the kind of undifferentiated wall of text nobody reads carefully. The final cut is the step most files skip, and it's the one that keeps the file from drifting back toward 'write clean code' by the fifth revision.

contentSections.body: Real commands, pointers to real files, repo-wide constraints, explicit prohibitions — and then cut anything that doesn't change what gets generated or reviewed.

title: When more context makes the output worse
description: Contradictory examples don't cancel out to something correct — they produce output that half-follows both, matching neither.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose output that blends two contradictory patterns from an overloaded context
Decide what to remove from a context bundle rather than only what to add

contentSections.title: Splitting the difference between two patterns

contentSections.body: Wanting to be thorough, a developer pastes the file tree, five example files, and a 3-page design doc into a prompt for one new function. Two of the five example files use conflicting error-handling styles — one from before a team-wide refactor, one after. The result: a function that throws for half its checks and returns a Result for the other half, matching neither style consistently.

contentSections.scenario: Two of five pasted example files actively disagree with each other about error-handling style, and nothing in the prompt says which one is current.
contentSections.question: What actually produced the inconsistent output?

options.label: Genuinely contradictory examples in the context, with no signal about which one is current, produced output that partially matches both rather than committing to either
The design doc confused the tool into writing worse code generally
A silent length limit was exceeded, corrupting part of the output

feedback.contradiction: Right. Contradictory patterns don't average out to something correct — they produce exactly the incoherent middle seen here, because nothing told the tool which one to actually follow. This is sharper than the routes.ts dilution problem from earlier in the module: it's not just noise crowding out a signal, it's two signals actively disagreeing.
feedback.doc-confused-it: The design doc is a plausible distraction but isn't what produced this specific symptom — a half-and-half blend of two concrete code patterns points specifically at the two conflicting example files, not at a prose document.
feedback.length-limit: Nothing here indicates truncation — the output is complete and coherent in form, just inconsistent in which convention it follows. That's a content problem, not a length problem.

contentSections.mechanism: More context can hurt in two distinct ways, and this is the second, sharper one. Dilution (the routes.ts example) buries a real signal under irrelevant noise. Contradiction actively confuses the tool about which of two real signals to follow, and the result is neither — a plausible-looking compromise that fully satisfies neither convention. The fix for dilution is a smaller bundle. The fix for contradiction is curation: remove the outdated file, or state explicitly which pattern is current and which is a holdover.

contentSections.body: Contradictory context doesn't average out — it produces output that half-follows both patterns and fully follows neither.

The instinct built across this whole module has mostly been about what to include. This lesson is the other half: reviewing a bundle for what to remove is a distinct step, not a smaller version of the same step. A file can be entirely accurate, entirely well-written, and still actively hurt this specific request — either by diluting the one file that matters, or by disagreeing with it.

contentSections.scenario: Before asking for rate limiting on one endpoint, a developer has assembled: the target endpoint's file, the existing rate limiter used elsewhere in the app, the project's full architecture design doc, and the complete 47-commit git history for the target file.
contentSections.question: Select every item that should be removed from this bundle before prompting.

items.label: The target endpoint's file
The existing rate limiter used elsewhere
The full architecture design doc
The complete 47-commit git history for the target file

explanation.target-file: Keep. This is the actual thing being changed — indispensable.
explanation.existing-limiter: Keep. This is the closest analog and the one file most likely to actually constrain a correctly-styled answer.
explanation.design-doc: Remove. Three pages of architecture context doesn't constrain what one rate-limiting function should look like, and its presence dilutes the two files that do.
explanation.commit-history: Remove. Forty-seven commits of history is background, not a constraint on this change — genuinely useful for understanding how the file evolved, not for writing one function correctly today.

contentSections.synthesis: Two files constrain the answer; two don't. Removing the two that don't isn't about saving space — it's the same dilution risk from earlier in the module, just applied as a subtraction step instead of an inclusion decision.

contentSections.body: Reviewing a bundle for what to remove is a separate step from deciding what to include — and it's the step most developers skip because it feels like undoing work they already did.

learningObjectives.text: Assemble a minimal, correctly-targeted context bundle for an unfamiliar repo at speed
Distinguish content that belongs in a project instruction file from content that doesn't
