title: Lab — Write the Project Instruction File for a Repo You Didn't Build
description: Write a real instruction file for an unfamiliar repository, then make the same kind of change twice — with and without it — and compare.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a project instruction file with commands, conventions, and prohibitions specific to a real repo
Compare AI-generated output produced with and without the instruction file

contentSections.body: The rest of this module argues that an instruction file earns its place by changing what gets generated. This lab tests that claim directly: write the file, then make the same kind of change with it and without it, and look at what's actually different.

contentSections.title: Instruction file, then a real comparison
contentSections.brief: Pick a repository you didn't build — an open-source project you use, a codebase from a previous job, or an unfamiliar corner of your own project you can approach fresh. Write its instruction file, then use it to make one small, real change twice: once with the file supplied as context, once without, using the same prompt otherwise.
contentSections.deliverable: The instruction file, and two generated diffs for the same small change — one made with the file, one without — with a short written comparison of what differed.

stages.title: Find the real commands and one real convention
stages.instructions: Locate the actual test, build, and lint commands from the repo's own config (package.json scripts, a Makefile, CI config) — not from memory or a README that might be stale. Then find one convention that's actually demonstrated consistently across at least two files, and note which files show it.
stages.checkpoint: You have exact, verified commands and one convention with named files that demonstrate it.

stages.title: Write the instruction file
stages.instructions: Write the file: commands, the convention with a pointer to a real file (not a prose re-description), any dependency or security defaults you can identify, and one explicit prohibition or flagged area if the repo has anything sensitive (a payments module, a migrations folder, an auth flow). Cut anything that doesn't constrain what gets generated.
stages.checkpoint: Every line names something checkable — a command, a pointer to a real file, a specific rule. Nothing reads as generic encouragement.

stages.title: Make the same change twice
stages.instructions: Pick one small, real change — a new function, a small endpoint, a utility. Prompt for it once with the instruction file supplied as context, and once in a fresh session with the same prompt but no instruction file. Keep both diffs.
stages.checkpoint: You have two diffs for the same requested change, produced under the two different conditions.

stages.title: Compare and self-check
stages.instructions: Write a short, specific comparison: what did the version with the instruction file get right that the other version didn't (or vice versa)? Point at actual lines, not a general impression. Then self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: The comparison names at least one concrete, specific difference traceable to something the instruction file stated.

rubric.criterion: Commands are verified, not assumed
rubric.meets: Pulled from the repo's actual config, not from a README or memory that could be stale.

rubric.criterion: The convention points at a real file
rubric.meets: Names a specific file and location, not a prose paraphrase of the pattern.

rubric.criterion: Every line is checkable
rubric.meets: No generic encouragement — a reader could verify whether each line was followed by looking at generated output.

rubric.criterion: The comparison is specific
rubric.meets: Points at actual lines or behaviors that differed, not a general 'the file helped' impression.

rubric.criterion: At least one difference traces to a specific instruction
rubric.meets: The comparison connects a concrete difference in the diffs back to a specific line in the instruction file.

contentSections.body: An instruction file's value isn't how thorough it sounds — it's whether the diff with it actually looks different from the diff without it, in a way you can point at.

title: Checkpoint — Context Is the Whole Job
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from The Executable Spec, two from further back. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions alongside earlier modules', without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Context Is the Whole Job

questions.from: This module — Context Is the Whole Job
questions.prompt: A fresh AI coding session is asked to follow "our patterns" with no file attached. What does it actually know about this repo's patterns?

options.label: Nothing — it has no standing access to your repo unless something is explicitly shown to it
Whatever it remembers from an earlier session with this developer
It can read the repo automatically because it's a coding tool

questions.explanation: There's no implicit channel by which repo conventions reach the tool — only what's explicitly placed in the session's context, session by session.

questions.from: This module — Context Is the Whole Job
questions.prompt: A relevant example file was pasted, but buried inside 2,000 mostly-irrelevant lines plus three unrelated files. The output ignored it. Why?

options.label: A relevant file present in a large, mostly-irrelevant dump carries no particular weight over anything else in it
The file was too large to process
Pasting unrelated files corrupts the relevant ones

questions.explanation: Present isn't the same as prominent. A small, specifically-targeted bundle makes the relevant pattern unmistakable; a large dump gives it no special status.

questions.from: This module — Context Is the Whole Job
questions.prompt: Why is a shown example file generally more reliable than a prose description for a convention with real control-flow shape?

options.label: A description can be true and still silently omit a specific case; a working example demonstrates the pattern at every point in its own logic
Prose instructions are always ignored by AI tools
Example files are shorter than descriptions

questions.explanation: The Result-type example followed the described convention everywhere except the one case the sentence never happened to address — a gap a full working example wouldn't have.

questions.from: This module — Context Is the Whole Job
questions.prompt: Two contradictory example files were both pasted into a prompt, with no signal about which was current. What did the output do?

options.label: Partially matched both patterns and fully matched neither
Correctly picked the more recent pattern on its own
Ignored both and used a third, unrelated pattern

questions.explanation: Contradictory signals don't average out to something correct — the result blended both inconsistently, because nothing told the tool which one to follow.

questions.prompt: Why does "make it better" fail as a spec?

options.label: It names no state the code could fail to be in, so nothing could be checked against it
It's too short
It doesn't mention a programming language

questions.explanation: A spec only does work if some output could fail it — 'better' can't fail, so it can't be confirmed either.

questions.prompt: Why write acceptance criteria before prompting rather than after seeing the code?

options.label: Criteria written against code already in front of you tend to bend toward describing what that code does
It's a required format for most tools
It makes the prompt shorter

questions.explanation: Criteria written first exist independent of any particular output, which is what lets them actually catch a gap instead of rationalizing one away.

questions.prompt: A spec line reads "handles the empty list case." What's wrong with it?

options.label: It names that a decision exists without recording what the decision was
It's too specific
Nothing — it's a complete edge case note

questions.explanation: A teammate with no memory of the original conversation could implement this two incompatible ways — it hasn't actually specified anything yet.

questions.prompt: A caching function's spec said "cache for a reasonable amount of time" and got implemented with no expiry at all. What was the actual failure?

options.label: "Reasonable" was never an actual duration — every reader fills in a different value
The developer who implemented it should have just known better
Caching functions are inherently hard to specify

questions.explanation: The fix is naming an exact number — 'TTL 300s' — the same length as the vague version but leaving nothing to fill in.

questions.from: Two modules back — What Actually Changes
questions.prompt: In Priya's rate-limiter session, what stayed with her rather than moving to the tool?

options.label: Deciding the counter should key on user id, and catching that the diff didn't
Typing the counter increment logic
Wiring the middleware into the route

questions.explanation: The decisions about correctness, and noticing when output doesn't match them, are exactly what didn't move to the tool.

questions.from: Two modules back — What Actually Changes
questions.prompt: What actually predicts whether a task is a good fit to delegate to an AI tool?

options.label: Pattern density and whether the result is checkable
How difficult the task looks to an experienced human
Whether the task involves a well-known algorithm

questions.explanation: A hard-looking regex can be a great fit; a trivial-sounding unwritten business rule can be a terrible one.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The first ninety seconds: what to look at first
description: Top-to-bottom reading spends the freshest attention on whatever happens to be first in the file. A fixed order front-loads the checks most likely to catch something expensive.

learningObjectives.text: Sequence a fast triage of a fresh diff that checks the highest-risk categories first
Explain why top-to-bottom reading under-weights behavioral risk

contentSections.title: A fixed order, not a scan

contentSections.body: A 200-line generated diff lands. Most reviewers start at line 1 and read down — naming, formatting, structure, the stuff that's easy to have an opinion about — and by the time they reach the wrong return value on line 180, the freshest part of their attention is long spent on things that were never going to hide a real defect.

Three questions, in this order, before a single line gets read for style: does it run at all — a crash or import error ends the review here, nothing else matters yet. Does the diff touch only what was actually requested — checkable by comparing the file and line list against the request, not by reading every line. Does one concrete, traced-by-hand input produce the right output — the fastest way to catch a wrong return value without reading the whole function. Style comes fourth, because it's real but doesn't determine whether anything above it was worth the time.

contentSections.question: Put the ninety-second triage in the order that front-loads the highest-risk checks.
steps: Confirm it runs without crashing or throwing an import error
Check the diff touches only what was actually requested
Trace one concrete input by hand and compare against the expected output
Read for style, naming, and formatting
contentSections.explanation: Runs-at-all is a gate, not a preference — nothing else is worth checking if this fails, so it goes first and can end the review immediately. Scope and a traced input are the two checks most likely to surface an expensive, easy-to-miss defect, and both are fast: scope is a comparison, not a read, and one traced input is minutes, not a full test suite. Style goes last because, unlike the first three, it doesn't change whether the code is a viable starting point — it only changes how much polish it needs once the starting point is confirmed sound.

contentSections.body: Runs, scope, one traced input — then style. In that order, because the first three determine whether the code is worth continuing to review at all.

Top-to-bottom reading isn't wrong because it's slow — it's wrong because it spends the scarcest resource in a review, fresh attention, on whatever happens to be first in the file, which has no reason to correlate with what's actually risky. A function's riskiest line is exactly as likely to be at line 180 as line 20, but a reviewer's attention is reliably higher at line 20 than line 180, purely from having read 160 lines in between.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer spends the first minute of a ninety-second review renaming two variables and fixing a formatting inconsistency near the top of a 200-line diff. By the time they reach a wrong return value on line 180, they've run out of the time they'd budgeted and approve the diff, planning to "look closer later."
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this outcome?

options.label: Attention was allocated by position in the file rather than by risk, so the highest-risk line got the least scrutiny purely because it came last
The reviewer was simply being careless
200 lines is inherently too long to review properly in ninety seconds

feedback.attention-misallocated: Right. Nothing about this reviewer's diligence changed between line 20 and line 180 — what changed was how much attention was left, and it ran out on a schedule set by file position, not by actual risk.
feedback.reviewer-careless: The reviewer spent real, careful effort — on the wrong things first. Carelessness isn't the mechanism; a misordered priority is.
feedback.diff-too-long: Length is a real constraint, but the fix demonstrated in this lesson doesn't require reading all 200 lines carefully — it requires spending the first minute on the three highest-value checks, which is possible regardless of length.

contentSections.mechanism: A review has a limited attention budget, and top-to-bottom reading allocates it by position instead of by risk — the first lines get the freshest scrutiny purely because they're first, with no guarantee that's where the risk actually is. The fixed order from this lesson exists specifically to break that correlation: runs-at-all, scope, and a traced input all get checked while attention is freshest, regardless of where in the file they happen to live.

contentSections.body: Attention spent by file position, not by risk, is spent on whatever happens to come first — which has no reason to be where the actual danger is.

title: Does it do the thing? Behaviour before style
description: A correct, ugly implementation is a fixable starting point. A wrong, beautiful one ships a bug that reads as trustworthy.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate two candidate implementations on behavior before style
Trace a boundary calculation by hand rather than judging it by how it reads

contentSections.title: Ugly and right beats clean and wrong

contentSections.body: Two candidate pagination helpers. Version A: clean, idiomatic, well-named — and returns `hasNextPage: true` on the actual last page, so the UI shows a working "next" button that leads nowhere. Version B: verbose, some awkward naming — and gets the boundary exactly right. Version A will get approved faster in a quick skim. Version B is the better foundation.

Style is cheap and reversible at any point — renaming, reformatting, restructuring for readability can happen after correctness is confirmed, at low cost. A wrong boundary condition is not reversible for free: it ships, it's used, and it's specifically dangerous when the surrounding code is clean, because fluency reads as trustworthiness to a reviewer moving quickly. This is the same fluency-versus-correctness gap from an earlier module, applied at the moment of triage rather than at the moment of writing the code.

contentSections.scenario: Version A and Version B of the pagination helper, as described above, are both candidates for a first-draft-to-refine decision.
contentSections.question: Which is the better first draft to build on?

options.label: Version B — correct and ugly is a fixable starting point; wrong and beautiful ships a trustworthy-looking bug
Version A — style problems compound faster than logic bugs over the life of a codebase
Roughly equivalent — style and correctness matter about the same amount at this stage

feedback.version-b: Right. What's wrong with B — names, verbosity — costs minutes to fix and never causes a silent failure. What's wrong with A ships a real defect, made more dangerous by looking like it doesn't need a second check.
feedback.version-a: This has it backwards for a first-draft decision specifically: style debt is visible and stays fixable indefinitely; a boundary bug is invisible exactly until it's hit in production, by which point it's much more expensive than a rename would ever have been.
feedback.equivalent: They're not equivalent at the triage stage — one candidate is a fixable foundation and the other is a defect wearing good clothes. They'd be closer to equivalent only once both are confirmed behaviorally correct.

contentSections.concept: At the first-draft stage, correctness and style aren't two items on the same list — they're different categories of risk. Style debt is bounded and fixable on your own schedule. A wrong boundary condition is unbounded until it's caught, and clean presentation actively works against catching it, because it lowers the reviewer's guard exactly where the guard matters most.

contentSections.body: Style debt is bounded and fixable later. A wrong boundary condition is unbounded until caught — and clean code makes it easier to miss, not harder.

The habit that actually catches boundary bugs: pick one concrete input at the boundary itself and compute the expression by hand, rather than reading the expression and judging whether it looks right. `(page * pageSize) < totalCount` looks exactly as plausible whether the comparison operator is `<` or `<=` — the only way to tell them apart is to plug in numbers.

contentSections.question: Quick check: could you tell, just by reading it without computing anything, whether `(page * pageSize) <= totalCount` is correct or has an off-by-one?
contentSections.hint: Both `<` and `<=` are completely ordinary, syntactically unremarkable comparison operators. Does either one look more 'correct' on sight?
contentSections.answer: No — neither operator looks more correct than the other by inspection; both are ordinary, valid comparisons that read as equally plausible. `<=` here would actually be wrong (it would report a next page on the true last page, since `2 * 10 <= 20` is true), but nothing about how it's written signals that. Plugging in the actual last-page numbers is the only way to tell — this is exactly why boundary conditions specifically need tracing, not reading.

contentSections.body: A boundary expression can't be judged by how it reads — `<` and `<=` look equally plausible sitting in the code. Plug in the actual boundary value and compute it.

title: Invented APIs, plausible names, and functions that don't exist
description: A method name can be exactly as plausible whether it's real, renamed, or never existed at all — and only checking against the actual installed version tells them apart.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an invented API from a version-drift failure
Verify a called method exists in the exact installed version rather than trusting how familiar it looks

contentSections.body: Generated JavaScript calls `items.groupByKey(item => item.category)`. No red underline in the editor — type checking isn't configured on this file. It runs, and throws: `TypeError: items.groupByKey is not a function`. The name reads exactly like a real method, because it's assembled from the shape of methods that actually exist elsewhere — Lodash has `groupBy`, other languages have close cousins — without ever having been a real JavaScript array method.

This is a distinct failure mode from a plain wrong answer: the code is syntactically valid, the method name is confident and well-formed, and it's assembled from genuinely common patterns in the training data — just not from this specific language's actual API surface. It happens most in exactly the situations you'd expect: a request that resembles a task common in a different language or library, or a codebase using several libraries whose conventions blend together in a plausible-sounding hybrid that belongs to none of them.

contentSections.question: What's actually wrong here, and what's the fix?

options.label: groupByKey isn't a real JavaScript array method — this will throw a TypeError the moment it runs
The arrow function syntax `item => item.category` is invalid
Object.entries() doesn't work on the result of a grouping operation

feedback.invented-method: Correct. No native JavaScript array method by this name exists. A real fix needs an actual grouping approach — a manual reduce, or `Object.groupBy` (a genuinely real, but recent, addition — worth checking the target runtime's version before relying on it) or a library like Lodash's real `groupBy`.
feedback.wrong-arrow-syntax: The arrow function itself is perfectly valid JavaScript — this isn't a syntax problem at all, which is part of what makes the actual bug easy to miss on a quick read.
feedback.object-entries-wrong: This line would work fine on a real plain object produced by an actual grouping operation — the problem happens one line earlier, before there's any grouped object to call Object.entries on at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The whole function reads as confident, idiomatic JavaScript, and every line except one is completely correct. The invented method is the kind of defect that survives a style-focused read entirely, because there's nothing stylistically off about it — the only way to catch it is checking whether the specific method actually exists on the specific type it's being called on, which a read for cleanliness doesn't do.

contentSections.body: A plausible-sounding method name proves nothing about whether it's real. Check the actual API surface, not how familiar the name looks.

contentSections.title: When the name used to be real

contentSections.scenario: Generated Python calls `pandas.DataFrame.append(row)`. It works fine on a developer's laptop (pandas 1.5 installed) and crashes in CI with `AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'append'` — CI runs pandas 2.0, where `.append()` was removed in favor of `pd.concat()`.
contentSections.question: How is this different from the invented `groupByKey` method from the previous section?

options.label: This method was genuinely real and common — the training data heavily reflects a version where it existed, and the failure is that it no longer exists in the specific version actually running, not that it was never real
This is the same failure as groupByKey — an invented name that was never real
The CI environment must be misconfigured if it can't find a standard pandas method

feedback.version-drift: Right. `.append()` was a real, extremely common pandas method for years — the training data reflects that heavily, and the local machine's older pandas version happened to mask the problem completely. This is version drift, not invention: the same underlying risk (an API surface that doesn't match reality) with a different specific cause.
feedback.same-thing: The distinction matters practically, even though the symptom (an AttributeError on a plausible method) looks similar: an invented name needs a genuinely different implementation, while a version-drifted one usually needs the modern equivalent of the same real operation — here, `pd.concat([df, pd.DataFrame([row])])`.
feedback.ci-misconfigured: CI is running the more current, and likely the actually-intended, pandas version. The 'misconfiguration' is really the mismatch between the developer's outdated local environment and the specification the tool should have been generating against.

contentSections.mechanism: Two different mechanisms produce the same symptom: a method call that fails because it doesn't exist in the version actually running. An invented method was never real in any version. A version-drifted method was real, often for a long time, and the training data's heavy representation of the older, more common pattern is exactly what makes the tool default to it. Both point at the same fix: check the called method against the exact installed version in the environment that will actually run the code, not against how familiar or common the name is.

contentSections.body: A method that used to be real and one that was never real produce the same crash. Either way, the fix is checking against the actual installed version, not against familiarity.

title: Silent scope creep: the changes you didn't ask for
description: A reviewer scanning for 'did it do what I asked' is primed to miss the unrelated changes riding along with it — and some of those cost more than the requested fix ever did.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish in-scope changes from scope creep in a real diff
Explain why scope creep is specifically likely to pass a scan focused on the requested change

contentSections.title: The comment nobody asked to remove

contentSections.body: The request: "fix the null check on `user.email` in `sendWelcomeEmail`." The diff fixes it. It also renames two unrelated parameters across the file, and deletes a comment reading `// workaround for legacy accounts, see TICKET-4021 — do not remove`. The requested fix is correct and easy to confirm. The deleted comment quietly removes the one thing that would have stopped someone, six months from now, from "cleaning up" the workaround it was protecting.

This connects back to an earlier module's mechanism — unscoped changes ride along because they're statistically common in the training data, not because the tool made a considered judgment — applied here as a review habit rather than a generation fact. A reviewer scanning for 'was the null check fixed' will confirm that it was, and that scan is specifically not primed to notice a deleted comment or a renamed parameter that has nothing to do with the null check. Scope creep is dangerous exactly because it hides behind a request that did get fulfilled correctly.

contentSections.scenario: The request: "add a 429 response when the rate limit is exceeded." Five lines from the actual diff.
contentSections.question: Select every line that's in scope — required by the request, or a direct necessary consequence of it.

items.label: Adds the 429 status code and Retry-After header when the limit is exceeded
Renames the middleware's internal counter variable from cnt to requestCount
Adds a new log line when the limit is exceeded, for observability
Changes the rate limit window from fixed to rolling
Updates the existing test to also check for the new 429 case

explanation.add-429: In scope. This is the requested behavior itself.
explanation.rename-counter: Scope creep. A plausible cleanup, and not what was asked — it rides along the way unrelated variable renames rode along with a rate-limiter fix in an earlier module.
explanation.add-log: Scope creep. Genuinely useful, and a separate decision from adding the 429 response — bundling it means it never gets its own review.
explanation.change-window: Scope creep, and the most dangerous of the three. This is a real behavioral change to something that wasn't part of the request, riding inside a diff that reads as 'just adding a status code.'
explanation.update-test: In scope. The existing test already covered this code path, and the request's own behavior needs coverage — this is a necessary consequence of the change, not an unrelated addition.

contentSections.synthesis: The two in-scope items are either the request itself or a direct requirement of it. All three scope-creep items are individually reasonable — that's exactly what makes them easy to wave through inside a diff that also does what was asked. The window-type change is the one worth remembering: it's a real behavioral change wearing the same clothes as a harmless drive-by rename.

contentSections.body: A diff that correctly does what was asked can still carry unrelated changes that ride along unnoticed — because the review is primed to check the request, not the rest.

The check that actually catches this: compare the list of changed files and lines against the request, explicitly, as its own step — not folded into a general read of the diff. Anything touched that the request doesn't account for gets a second look on its own terms, regardless of how small or reasonable it looks.

contentSections.question: Quick check: would a reviewer who only asks 'does this correctly add the 429 response?' catch the rolling-window change from the earlier example?
contentSections.hint: That question is specifically about whether the request was fulfilled. Is the window-type change relevant to answering it?
contentSections.answer: No — that question would get answered 'yes,' correctly, and the window-type change simply isn't part of what it's asking about. It takes a second, separate question — 'does this diff touch anything the request didn't ask for?' — to surface it. This is exactly why scope has to be its own explicit check, not a question folded into 'did it work.'

contentSections.body: Diff the changed lines against the request as its own explicit step. Anything left over gets reviewed on its own terms, no matter how small it looks.

title: The refine-or-restart call, and why restarting is usually cheaper
description: Three symptoms with one shared root cause mean the foundation is wrong, not the details — and refining a wrong foundation just produces a fourth symptom.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether repeated refinement failures share a structural cause
Decide between refining and restarting using a stated distinction rather than a gut call

contentSections.body: Three rounds of "try again" on a caching layer. Round one: a stale-read bug. The fix produces round two: a memory leak. That fix produces round three: a race condition. All three trace back to the very first draft's core decision — caching at the per-request layer instead of per-session. Each fix genuinely addressed that round's symptom. None of them touched the actual cause, which is why there was always going to be a fourth symptom.

contentSections.scenario: The caching layer from the hook: three rounds, three different symptoms, one shared root cause never addressed.
contentSections.question: What does this pattern indicate about whether to refine again?

options.label: The foundational approach was wrong from round one — each refinement patches a new symptom of the same structural problem rather than fixing it
The tool is having an unlucky run and a fourth attempt is likely to work
Caching is inherently too hard to specify, regardless of approach

feedback.wrong-foundation: Right, and this is the specific signal worth learning to recognize: not that attempts are failing, but that the failures keep sharing a root cause while wearing different symptoms. Each fix is locally correct and globally useless, because it never reaches the actual problem.
feedback.bad-luck: There's no mechanism by which the fourth round becomes luckier than the third if the underlying architecture is unchanged — the pattern of shared root cause predicts another symptom, not a resolution.
feedback.too-complex: The per-session redesign in the resolved version of this scenario isn't more complex than the per-request version that produced three bugs — it's a different, more appropriate structure. Complexity isn't the variable that mattered here.

contentSections.mechanism: The diagnostic move is checking whether repeated failures share a cause, not just counting how many rounds have failed. Two unrelated bugs in two rounds is still refine-worthy — that's the normal shape of iterative correction. Two or more bugs that trace to the same structural decision is the restart signal, because refining within a structure that can't support the requirement will keep producing new symptoms of the same gap, at a cost that adds up faster than a restart from a better foundation would have.

contentSections.body: Check whether failures share a cause before deciding to refine again. A repeating root cause behind different symptoms means the foundation is wrong, not the details.

Two rounds in is rarely enough to be certain, which is exactly when the habit matters most: before requesting a third refinement, trace whether the new bug shares a cause with the old one. If it does, that's evidence toward restarting with a different structural approach stated explicitly in the next prompt — not just "try again," but naming what changed and why.
Before a third refinement, check whether the new bug and the old one share a cause. If they do, restart with the structural problem named — don't just ask again.

title: Lab — Triage a Backlog of Six Generated Changes
description: Apply the module's whole framework to six real or realistic generated diffs, and produce a triage table a teammate could act on without re-deriving your reasoning.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the ninety-second triage and refine/restart distinction across a batch of real changes
Justify a refine/rewrite/discard verdict for each with a specific, checkable reason

contentSections.body: Real review queues don't arrive one diff at a time with unlimited attention for each. This lab is closer to the real job: six generated changes, a fixed triage method, and a table someone else could read and trust without watching you work.

contentSections.title: Triage six generated changes
contentSections.brief: Gather six generated diffs — from your own recent AI-assisted work, from a public PR queue where AI-generated changes are labeled, or a mix of real ones and ones you deliberately generate for this lab from six different small requests. For each, run the module's triage and record a refine, rewrite, or discard verdict.
contentSections.deliverable: A table: six diffs, each with a runs/scope/traced-input verdict, a refine-or-restart call where relevant, and a one-line reason a teammate could act on without re-deriving your judgment.

stages.title: Assemble six diffs and their original requests
stages.instructions: Gather six generated changes, each with the request that produced it. Vary them if you can — at least one should be behaviorally correct, at least one should have a real defect, and if possible at least one should show scope creep or an invented API, so the lab exercises the whole framework rather than one corner of it.
stages.checkpoint: Six diffs, each with its original request stated alongside it.

stages.title: Run the ninety-second triage on each
stages.instructions: For each diff: confirm it runs, check scope against the request, and trace one concrete input by hand. Record the result of each of the three checks individually — not just a final impression.
stages.checkpoint: Each of the six diffs has three recorded results: runs (yes/no), scope (clean/creep, with what crept if any), and the traced input's outcome.

stages.title: Call refine, rewrite, or discard
stages.instructions: For anything that didn't pass cleanly, decide: refine (a fixable, isolated issue), rewrite (the approach is fundamentally wrong, per this module's structural-cause test — even on a first pass, ask whether the issue looks like a symptom of a deeper structural mismatch), or discard (not worth continuing with at all, worth just doing manually). State the reason in terms this module actually taught, not a vague impression.
stages.checkpoint: Every diff has a verdict, and the reason names a specific check it failed or passed — 'scope creep in the window-type change' rather than 'seemed off.'

stages.title: Compile the table and self-check
stages.instructions: Compile all six into one table a teammate could read cold. Then self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: A colleague reading only the table would understand every verdict without asking you to explain it.

rubric.criterion: All three ninety-second checks are recorded per diff, not just a final impression
rubric.meets: Runs, scope, and traced-input results are each stated individually for all six.

rubric.criterion: At least one scope-creep or invented-API case is caught and named specifically
rubric.meets: Names the exact unrelated change or invented call, not a general 'looked risky.'

rubric.criterion: Every verdict has a specific, checkable reason
rubric.meets: The reason references an actual check result, not a gut feeling — a colleague could verify it independently.

rubric.criterion: Refine vs. restart calls use the structural-cause test
rubric.meets: Any restart call states what structural issue makes refining unlikely to work, not just 'it's pretty broken.'

rubric.criterion: The table is usable without you in the room
rubric.meets: A colleague could act on every row without asking a follow-up question.

contentSections.body: A verdict without a specific, checkable reason is a gut feeling with a label on it. The table's whole value is that someone else could trust it without re-deriving your judgment.
